subtopic: MR. COLDWELL  LETTER FROM CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY RESPECTING NEW TRAIN AND ISSUANCE OF PASSES THEREFOR
MR. COLDWELL  LETTER FROM CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY RESPECTING NEW TRAIN AND ISSUANCE OF PASSES THEREFOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I think affects the privileges of all members of the house and the members of the other place. There has been placed on my desk a copy of a letter to the Clerk of the House from the Canadian Pacific Railway which I should like to read. It is dated April 15, 1955, and is as follows:
Dear Mr. Raymond:
As you know, Canadian Pacific on April 24 next will, through the Canadian, trains 1, 2, 11 and 12, inaugurate a new standard of passenger transportation in Canada. The reception of this new endeavour of Canadian Pacific by the travelling public has been most gratifying and advance reservations indicate that the demand will often exceed the space available.
In light of the large investment of the company in the new equipment and the demand for space, it has been decided that where possible the Canadian will be used exclusively for revenue passengers. Restrictions are being placed on all passes issued by Canadian Pacific.
Under section 351 of the Railway Act, the company is required to honour free transportation issued by you pursuant to that section on any trains of the company. Canadian Pacific cannot, therefore, restrict free transportation issued to senators, members of the House of Commons and members and staff of the board. We would, therefore, ask your co-operation in bringing to the attention of all to whom you issue free transportation certificates the necessity as far as possible of ensuring that the train be made available for revenue passengers. This co-operation by members of the Senate, House of Commons and by the board will not impose too great an inconvenience in that the present transcontinental train, the Dominion, which is designated Nos. 7 and 8, will continue to operate on a high standard of service providing an opportunity for a comfortable and enjoyable journey across Canada.
Sincerely yours,
N. R. Crump, Vice-President.
I raise this as a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, because the Railway Act is quite clear. The Canadian Pacific Railway, in common with other railways, receives certain concessions from parliament, and to send a letter of this description to the Clerk of the House of Commons to be conveyed to members of the house is in effect an attempt to infringe upon the right which we have under
the Railway Act. I respectfully suggest that the Clerk should ignore the contents of the letter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the house that a settlement of the dispute affecting terminal elevator employees at the lakehead was reached this morning. I know that our news service is so efficient that this information has reached hon. members before now, but I think in closing this matter I should place upon the record the terms of the settlement.
The terms tentatively agreed upon yesterday in the negotiations between the parties conducted before the industrial inquiry commissioner, Mr. Eric Taylor, who was appointed by my department last week, were approved by the members of the brotherhood at a meeting held this morning. The terms of settlement are as follows:
Period of Contract: January 1, 1954, to December 31, 1956.

Labour Conditions
Wages: Effective January 1, 1954, 5 cents per hour additional.
Effective October 1, 1954, 3 cents per hour additional.
Effective January 1, 1955, 2 cents per hour additional.
Effective January 1, 1956, 2 cents per hour additional.
Statutory Holidays: Two extra days with pay if not worked, making a total of eight such holidays in the calendar year.
Health and Welfare: Blue Cross medical plan on a 50-50 basis, effective May 1, 1955. The monthly contribution by the employers to this fund is $3.50 and the same amount by the employees.
The new contract will contain the following additional provisions: (a) a provision setting out the rights of management; (b) a provision prohibiting strikes or lockouts during the period of the contract; (c) a provision for a more modern procedure with respect to the settlement of grievances; (d) a provision defining probationary employment.
I should like to express appreciation for the sensible and sincere manner in which, in the last 48 hours, the two parties to the dispute have dealt with this matter, resulting in this settlement, which enables the movement of a particularly sensitive product of Canada at this time. I also wish to pay tribute to the mediator and to the senior officials of my own department for their work in connection with the case.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED UNEMPLOYMENT CONDITION AT SEVEN ISLANDS, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asked me a question regarding the assembly of new Canadians who are unemployed at Seven Islands, Quebec. At that time I gave him an immediate reply based upon my memory of a tentative report we then had. I should like now to make some correction in the reply I gave on that date. I am particularly speaking of this matter again in view of a dispatch which appeared in this morning's Gazette.

Since seeing that dispatch I have asked our director of employment to get in touch with the situation directly and immediately, and this is his report to me at noon today. He
says:
I got in touch with Mr. Simard, local office manager, unemployment insurance commission, by telephone.
Following our investigations last week he made a thorough study of the situation and he reported to me there are 448 unemployed people registered in his office. Of this number, 120 are designated by him personally as immigrants.
That is the special correction I wish to make with regard to my own statement. I said the other day that it was 80, as it appeared to me to be at that time. He goes on to say:
He had no easy way, of course, of ascertaining whether or not these workers were immigrants but he used this method. He had the leaders get together the various ethnic groups and they came to his office and registered. These were as a consequence designated by Mr. Simard as the immigrants under discussion.
It developed that there were a total of 120. This is an increase over the figure of 80 that was at first estimated. However 50 per cent of the 120-again this is an estimate-are former iron ore company employees who would ordinarily be called back on a seniority basis. They returned to Seven Islands earlier without being called back and as a consequence are still out of work and may be until May 15.
Twenty-three of the 120 are of Greek origin and were brought to Seven Islands by a Greek society. Of this group, only one has been in Canada less than a year.
Mr. Simard reports further that of the 120 about 60 of them are drawing unemployment insurance benefits.
He emphasizes the fact that there are not 600 immigrants involved in this problem and actually the 23 Greeks are the only ones that seem to be short of funds and steps are being taken to see that they do not suffer hardships.
Mr. Simard emphasizes that there is no crowding around the unemployment insurance commission office and that everything is completely under control.

subtopic: LOSS-LEADER SELLING  TABLING OF REPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LOSS-LEADER SELLING  TABLING OF REPORT
speechtext:
I wish to table the report of the restrictive trade practices commission of an inquiry into loss-leader selling.
Hon. members will remember that, when legislation forbidding the practice of resale price maintenance was recommended by the MacQuarrie committee and enacted by parliament, fears were expressed in some business quarters that the abolition of resale price maintenance would lead to an increase of so-called loss-leader selling. It was feared that this would have certain harmful effects both on retailers and on manufacturers. The MacQuarrie committee therefore recommended that an inquiry be made into the prevalence and effects of loss-leader selling with

a view to recommending suitable legislation, if any were considered necessary, to deal with it. The government, also, when the legislation forbidding resale price maintenance was being debated, promised to give close attention to its effects and to any practices which might develop as a result of it to any further legislative action that might, therefore, seem appropriate. The inquiry into loss-leader selling was in pursuance of these considerations.
The report, which the government is now engaged in studying, expresses the opinion that the practice of loss-leader selling does not call for legislative action at the present time.
Copies of the report in English are being distributed to members by the joint distribution branch. Owing to the length of the report, the French edition is not yet ready. Translations of the introductory and conclusion chapters are available and are being distributed by the joint distribution branch. The complete French edition will be distributed at the earliest possible date.

On Monday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton asked a question with regard to employment in the car repair shops at Leaside. The hon. members for York-Scarborough, Spadina and York East have also discussed the same matter with me. After receiving these inquiries I obtained from the management of the Canadian National Railways the following information:
In examining maintenance requirements for rolling stock the management came to the conclusion that substantial economies and greater efficiency of operation could be realized by transferring car repair work to other railway shops with modern equipment and plant lay-out already available and currently not used to capacity. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO CRASHES OF T-33 AIRCRAFT IN MANITOBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. Since 19 lives have been lost in 20 crashes of T-33 aircraft during the last year in Manitoba, is the air force contemplating grounding T-33's pending an investigation as to whether the aircraft is to blame, or the methods of training. Are any changes in administration contemplated in Manitoba stations?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO CRASHES OF T-33 AIRCRAFT IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. May I say at the outset that I do not agree with the suggestion contained in the latter part of his question, that either lack of airworthiness of the aircraft or the method of training is responsible for the accidents which have taken place.
2994	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry Naturally the Royal Canadian Air Force and the department are very much concerned with any accidents which result in loss of life. But, as I said, in answer to a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member, the answer to which appears at page 2431 of Hansard for March 28 last, our aircraft accident rate in Canada compares very favourably with those of the United States and the United Kingdom.
With respect to the T-33 crashes which have taken place in Canada, I may say that it is routine practice for expert R.C.A.F. accident investigators to investigate each specific accident thoroughly. This has been done in respect of each T-33 crash. After a careful reconstruction of each crash, in so far as it was possible, the Royal Canadian Air Force is convinced that no pattern has emerged from these accidents which would indicate any structural defects or any lack of airworthiness in the aircraft. There is therefore no appreciable reason why the aircraft should be grounded. As a matter of fact the T-33 has had a long and very good record of service both in the United States and in Canada.
Instructional techniques employed by the Royal Canadian Air Force have gone through a long and gradual evolution and are similar to and in some respects are considered superior to methods employed by other major air forces.
I might also add that the concentration of T-33 accidents in Manitoba is probably not unrelated to the fact that practically all T-33 flying training and weapons training in the Royal Canadian Air Force is being carried out in Manitoba. The scope of this training can be judged when I mention that there are several hundreds of T-33's involved.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF SALK VACCINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, which is a follow-up to my question to him on March 7 last. Has the government, in cooperation with the provinces, any plans to take over or take part in the distribution of the proven Salk poliomyelitis vaccine, which is shortly to be available on the Canadian market through commercial drug houses, in the same manner as it is doing with the supply of the Connaught laboratories of Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF SALK VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mackenzie has given me notice of a question which I think in some particulars is the same as the question which my hon. friend has just asked me. The hon. gentleman who has just put his question did not give me notice of the specific question and consequently in fairness I feel that I should refer to the hon. member for Mackenzie.
The federal government, of course, has no control in so far as control of the distribution of products of any commercial organization is concerned. It is true that the Minister of National Health and Welfare did give a licence to two commercial companies, but that licence had to do with the testing of the potency and the safety of the particular vaccine. It will be a matter for provincial action as to whether or not there should be in any way control directed over the distribution in a province of a company. However, I think the question presupposes facts that are not really the case. It should be understood that the only sources of supply of the vaccine in the United States will be the commercial companies. That is not the case in Canada. The main source of supply for some time will be the Connaught laboratories at the University of Toronto, and within a very short time as well the institute of microbiology at the University of Montreal. I cannot say exactly when the commercial product

will be available, although perhaps one company now is in the process of distributing, in certain parts of Canada, some small quantities of the vaccine.
Whatever control is being arranged has already been provided for as a result of a decision made by the ten provinces and the federal government last fall before the full value of the vaccine was made known. As a result of those prearrangements, I believe there will be in Canada as great a measure of control providing for the availability of this vaccine as exists in any other jurisdiction in the world at the present time. Much credit for this should go to the provinces and to the federal government who were able to make this arrangement, and I should like to say particularly to the Connaught laboratories who have played such a distinguished role in this very important matter.
As I have said publicly, great credit for the vaccine must go primarily to Dr. Salk, but if it had not been for the role of the Connaught laboratories, success in Canada would not have been attained so early. In view of the historic character of this particular discovery, I thought I should in this house mention particularly in grateful acknowledgment the services of Dr. Defries, of the Connaught laboratories, and particularly the researches of Dr. Rhodes, Dr. Joseph Morgan, Miss Helen Morton and Dr. Parker, all of the Connaught laboratories.
I am happy to say, Mr. Speaker, that Dr. Morgan, who was a member of the research team that discovered medium 199, which is so essential to the preparation of the vaccine, is at the present time, along with Miss Morton, a valued servant of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
This vaccine will be available in Canada in as great a quantity during the next two or three months as will be the case anywhere in the world. I expect that one-

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Mae-donnell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I wish to speak to two specific subjects, one having to do with the Department of Agriculture and one having to do with the Department of National Revenue. Before proceeding to deal with those matters I should like to make a few general comments with respect to the budget which is now before us.
On careful reading of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) one is struck almost immediately with the number of "ifs" contained in the budget. For this reason it could be called the "if" budget, and therefore I think hon. members generally will find it rather difficult to discuss the budget. A great number of unknown factors were contained in the analysis and

proposals of the minister. However, there were some things specifically stated and I should like to draw attention to one or two of these.
In my opinion one of the glaring omissions from the budget proposals is the almost complete lack of any provision for the primary producers of this country. With the exception of a few minor changes in the tariff structure having to do with certain equipment imported for farming purposes, there is almost a blank-out of any reference to any change which would be of benefit to agriculture generally. The few changes which are provided in the tariff structure for the benefit of agricultural producers I think are more than offset by one provision which will be included in the budget proposals if the minister carries out his expressed intention of increasing the tariff on ethylene glycol.
If as a result of the study made by the tariff board the government goes through with this increase it will do more harm to agricultural producers than the total of the concessions which have been made through the reduction of the tariff on certain items. I certainly hope that the minister will not recommend to this house any increase in the duty on that commodity because the differential between the Canadian and United States prices is already considerable and the only effect of any increase would be to increase the price to the consumer in Canada. As the minister knows, with mechanized farming this is a commodity which enters definitely into the cost of production.
The other matter to which I want to make reference is the reducing of the tax on corporations. The minister was only carrying out a broad hint which he made last month in Montreal, in which he indicated that the tax on corporations was too high, and he therefore took steps to reduce it in the higher brackets. But I cannot be too enthusiastic about the reductions in the individual income tax, because it seems to me that the reductions in dollars are being made for those who least require them; in other words, the ones who needed the relief from taxation the most got the least consideration.
If I read correctly the table placed on record by the minister in regard to single taxpayers, table III at the top of page 2736, I find this. If he is earning $1,500 he will pay $5 less in 1955 than he paid in 1954. If we jump to $3,000, we find he will save $20 in taxation. If we jump to $10,000 income, he will save $90. If we jump further to $50,000, he will save $490. Then if we jump to $400,000, he will save $3,990. In dollars and cents, that means that a person with an
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny income of half a million dollars will get as much tax relief as 800 single persons earning $1,500 a year. In my opinion that is going about it in altogether the wrong way. If it is the intention of the minister in making these tax reductions to increase the purchasing power of the Canadian public-I would assume that would be the chief consideration, as I can think of no other one which would be more valuable-then by relieving the person with an income of half a million dollars by almost $4,000, he is not increasing his purchasing power in the normal sense, because that person is already able to buy everything he requires with the income he has. He is giving him a tax reduction equal to that of 800 persons in the $1,500 bracket. In my opinion, the more equitable way to have done it would have been to raise the exemption level and make the necessary adjustments in the rates in the higher brackets in order that all the benefit of the raising of the exemption level would come to the persons in the lower income groups. Not only would that provide them with a greater amount of purchasing power generally, but it would also save the Minister of National Revenue a great deal of headaches and administrative expense, because he would have immediately perhaps tens of thousands less income tax forms to process; if you raise the exemption level, there will automatically be a large number of persons who have no longer to be taxed.
I think that would be a fairer and more effective method of providing tax relief for those who need it most, and it would be of benefit to the whole economy if it were done that way. However, the minister has chosen this way, and quite obviously it is a shift to the right: reduction in taxation for the big corporations and big reductions in income tax for the people with big incomes, but practically peanuts for the ones in the lower income groups.
While there has been some relief from taxation for certain groups, there is one group, as a matter of fact, which as a result of the budget proposals is facing a serious loss, and I wish to say a word on that today. I refer to the automobile dealers who are stocked now with new cars, for which they have already paid, including the excise taxes. They should receive some consideration with respect to a refund on the tax they have paid, to the extent of the reduction of the excise tax. Perhaps the government is not aware that in the last few years the automobile dealers have been put into an entirely different position from that which they used to occupy with respect to the automobile manufacturers. It used to be possible for an

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny automobile dealer to obtain a number of new cars on what was known as consignment. In other words, he did not have to pay for them in cash; the cars were shipped to him, and if he was able to sell them he paid the company within a certain length of time. Now the situation is different. Owing to the credit restrictions which have been imposed in recent years on the dealers, the dealers are now obliged to pay cash on delivery for the automobiles they order. Automobile dealers who now have new cars in stock will have to pay for them, including the tax. There is no provision for them to return these automobiles to the manufacturer; they are bought and paid for. They are in the position of having to lose between $135 and $150 per unit, at a time when they have had a few years of not very active business. I would hope that the government would reconsider the decision announced the other day by the Minister of Finance and endorsed by the Minister of National Revenue yesterday. I think that is one group which will face serious loss unless some consideration is shown.
Now I come to the particular matters which I wish to discuss today. The first one has to do with the question of public investment. I am going to narrow down the subject in this case to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I do that for a particular purpose. This house has debated on one or two occasions resolutions moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West dealing with the national conservation program, and in my opinion it would be very desirable. Until we are prepared to make such a move there is now on the statute books an act enacted in 1935 and amended in 1937 and again in 1951, known as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which has to do with the three prairie provinces and the Peace River block in British Columbia. Now under section 4 of this act the minister is given certain authority with the advice of the advisory board to do certain reclamation work, drainage, reforestation, and so forth, in order to prevent soil erosion. In another part of the act, under section 9, the minister is given conditional powers under which he can enter into an agreement with prairie provinces and municipalities in order to do special projects in those areas outside of the area designated in the act.
I should perhaps point out that under the act now the prairie farm rehabilitation board has jurisdiction in an area roughly known as the Palliser triangle, which takes in the southwest portion of Manitoba, more than half the province of Saskatchewan, and the southeast portion of the province of Alberta with a strip going north on the west side.

That leaves out of the jurisdiction of the board a large portion of the province of Manitoba particularly.
We have found that over the years efforts have been made to have the provisions of that act applied to all settled areas in the three prairie provinces, and as a matter of fact in the four western provinces. In May of last year the four ministers of agriculture of the four western provinces had a joint conference dealing with this matter, and in a Canadian Press dispatch dated 10th May, 1954, the following news item appeared, and I quote:
Regina. A recommendation that the prairie farm rehabilitation administration's area of operations be extended to cover all agricultural lands in the four western provinces has been made by the agriculture ministers of these provinces.
Referring to the four provinces.
The recommendation was contained in a joint statement released by Saskatchewan agriculture minister, I. C. Nollet, at the end of a two-day conference of the ministers here Friday. The statement said the conference agreed "the work of the P.F.R.A. has been an important factor in helping stabilize agricultural production in the areas where it has been applied.
The ministers noted that many of the areas outside of the P.F.R.A. boundary in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia were in similar need of the P.F.R.A. policies.
That was on the 10th of May. In another dispatch of the same date which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press reference is made to a statement made by the minister of agriculture of Manitoba, the Hon. R. D. Robertson. The article reads in part as follows:
This decision was made at the conference of provincial agricultural ministers and their deputies in Regina last week.
The reference is to the decision to ask the government to extend the provisions of the act.
"The fact that we're all agreed P.F.R.A. should be extended strengthens all our hands." ... At present the P.F.R.A. area coincides approximately with the Palliser triangle and in addition there is the Peace river block.
On the 7th of June last year I wrote a letter to the Minister of Agriculture following a number of conversations we had had about the matter in which I asked whether any action would be taken last year to carry out the requests of the ministers of agriculture of the four western provinces. In his reply dated June 9 he had this to say:
The only area which has been singled out for activities under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act is what is fairly well defined as the Palliser triangle. Anything which is done in the areas outside the Palliser triangle, which is similar to the work done under P.F.R.A., is provided for under special votes which appear in my estimates each year.
Then he ended with this paragraph, and it is rather important:
It has not been thought advisable to assume what the constitution attributes to the provinces, at

least until a final and permanent agreement has been reached between the federal and the provincial governments with regard to financing in general. It is therefore not the intention to introduce legislation during this session.
That was last year. The reason I bring up the matter now and treat it as one of importance is in view of the fact that a dominion-provincial conference is to be held very soon, and it is quite possible this is one of the matters which may be considered. I think it is time that some decision was arrived at because repeated requests have been made by these provinces. We have in the prairie provinces a soil erosion problem which is far more urgent than anywhere else in Canada. It is partly due to the type of farming carried on and partly to the climatic conditions. Soil erosion, resulting in some cases from not enough rain and in other cases from too much rain, is causing damage and loss of fertility running into millions of dollars, and I think it is certainly time to apply public investment to a wasting asset which cannot be replaced.
Once the topsoil is washed down streams or blown away by the winds we have lost the most fertile and valuable part of our farming land. That is a process which has been going on for some time. I speak particularly about the province of Manitoba. If I were to say in the house that the government has discriminated against the province of Manitoba with relation to this act I might be accused of being partisan about the question, but I am going to quote the words of Liberal members of the Manitoba provincial house. Certainly the government would not accuse them of being partisan to their disadvantage. For example, on the 18th of January of this year a report appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press concerning a discussion by Mr. Hill-house, the Liberal member for St. Andrews, of this very question of the application of the rehabilitation act in Manitoba. He had some rather strong criticisms to make of the federal government and particularly the Minister of Agriculture. The article reads in part as follows:
He said, during the Selkirk federal by-election last fall, Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, had promised $1 million in federal aid for flood alleviation in the interlake area. However, Mr. Hillhouse said, the amount Ottawa was offering had now shrunk to $125,000 . . .
As a matter of fact, up till now no agreement has been signed between the federal government and the province of Manitoba for any amount of money. These are the kind of things about which we are complaining. When a senior minister of the crown like the Minister of Agriculture goes to a point in Manitoba to speak at an important
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny public meeting and makes the statement there that he is willing to recommend to the government that $1 million be granted, and nothing is done about it, we have reason to complain. As a matter of fact, it was $1,500000 to start with, then it came down to $1 million and then all the way down to $125,000.
There is an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 8 dealing with the remarks of another Liberal member of the provincial house, Mr. Gildas Molgat, member for Ste. Rose. That happens to be part of my federal constituency and I know him very well. The article reads in part as follows:
Earlier Gildas Molgat, Liberal, Ste. Rose, said his area had been hard hit by floods since 1947 and that the P.F.R.A. "is not doing its job".
This is a Liberal member of the legislature making this statement. Then the article continues:
He charged the federal government with "discrimination" against Manitoba in framing the act. and urged that the province "put more pressure on" for amendments to P.F.R.A. so that it would cover all settled areas of the west and place "proper responsibility" on the dominion for damage done by drainage from federal park areas.
He was referring there of course to the Riding Mountain national park which is one of the sources of many of our flood problems in that part of Manitoba. So it goes all down the line. Again, in an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 8 you will find the following report of what the minister of agriculture of Manitoba, Mr. Robertson, had said. The article reads:
Mr. Robertson admitted that Mr. Gardiner may have made such a statement-
He was referring to the promise of $1 million.
-but that the deal had not been settled and that the province had insisted that any work affecting the level of the lakes was 100 per cent federal responsibility.
There you have a situation where Liberal members in the provincial house of Manitoba, including cabinet ministers, stand up and say that it is the responsibility of the federal government to carry out these over-all projects which would prevent the flood situations we have had. Yet the Minister of Agriculture states in this chamber that he will not recommend legislation because-and I quote from his letter-"it has not been thought advisable to assume what the constitution attributes to the provinces".
We cannot have it both ways. Either it is the responsibility of the provinces or of the federal government, and if there is any doubt about it then the dominion-provincial conference is the proper place to settle these doubts so that agreement can be reached. I think it is time some action was taken instead of having a lot of promises made at strategic

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny times, usually when there is an election somewhere in the offing. I leave it at that. I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is not present today but I am sure that my comments will be brought to his attention.
The other matter to which I want to make reference today has to do with the Department of National Revenue. As my text for what I wish to say I want to take a statement made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech which will be found at page 2739 of Hansard of April 5. At that time he stated:
May I say at this point, Mr. Speaker, what I think all hon. members know, that the Minister of Finance imposes and receives taxes. It is the duty of the Minister of National Revenue and his department to collect them. I should like to express my thanks to him and to his officials for the efficient and impartial manner in which this duty is discharged.
I have no objection whatever to one minister of the crown paying a compliment to a colleague. It is only a matter of professional courtesy that he should do so. I am not quite sure that he was not a little premature in his congratulations because frankly I am not impressed with some of the methods the Department of National Revenue has employed in the collection of taxes. I raised this question, which I am going to raise today, on another occasion, on March 4, in a debate in this house. While I set out the facts as I have them, and repeatedly asked the government to make some statement about them, when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) replied in that debate he made no reference whatever to the statement I had made. Now, either he was not aware of those statements or he chose to disregard them. Whichever was the case, I am going to give him another opportunity today or during the course of this debate to explain the situation which I brought before the house at that time.
I am referring again to the matter of tax remissions made under the authority of the Financial Administration Act, and on the recommendation no doubt of the Department of National Revenue or the treasury board, to four corporations, namely the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, which received a remission of $549,000, in round figures; the Gatineau Power Company, $496,000; the Saguenay Power Company Limited, $576,000; and the Bell Telephone Company, $371,000. The exact total of these remissions is $1,992,728.11, or very close to $2 million.
Now, the circumstances under which these remissions were made appear to me to be quite unjustified. I stated the facts previously, and I am going to state them again. As a matter of fact, on the basis of another

return which has come to my hand since then, I find that the information contained in the original return or sessional paper No. 99-B in reply to my question of February 14, was not correct. I am not going to accuse the Department of National Revenue of deliberately making a false return because they are very insistent that taxpayers should not do that. There are penalties provided for the making of false returns. But I do say the department made a quite inaccurate return; whether or not it was deliberate I cannot say. The facts stated in the first return do not agree with the facts stated in the later return on the same subject which came to my hand on March 28, 1955. I shall point out the differences in a moment.
When I raised this matter before, I pointed out that the dispute between these four companies and the department arose over a tax liability which the companies claimed they should not pay. The question arose as a result of the Quebec education tax which was imposed in 1946. The four companies which I have mentioned claimed that they should receive a deduction with respect to the education tax they paid to Quebec. The Department of National Revenue held that they would have to pay their full liability. In my opinion the department was quite justified in their attitude. If we refer to the Income Tax Act, section 12, we find the following:
In computing income, no deduction shall be made in respect of
(g) a corporation tax, as defined by regulation, paid to the government of a province or to a municipality . . .
Well, th.ere is not much doubt as to the meaning of that. On the basis of that section the department, I think quite properly, turned down the claim of the four companies and insisted that the tax be paid. The companies decided to appeal to the income tax appeal board, and here is where we find one of the differences between the two returns that are received. The original return stated that the matter was submitted to the income tax appeal board and the board decided that the tax in question was deductible. Then the return states that on appeal to the exchequer court the board's decision was reversed. All this information refers to these four companies.
Upon looking at the second return I find that, as a matter of fact, two of the companies did not even appeal to the income tax appeal board and that with respect to them, there was no appeal made from that board to the exchequer court. Those companies were the Aluminum Company of Canada

Limited and the Bell Telephone Company.
I quote these words from the second return:
Regarding the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited and the Bell Telephone Company of Canada it may be said that these two companies filed appeals from the disallowance of the Quebec education tax as a deduction from income.
The question in issue was similar to the one raised in the appeals of Gatineau Power Company and Saguenay Power Company Limited. In view of the fact that these latter appeals had previously been heard by the income tax appeal board and by the exchequer court, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada and the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited requested, and the crown agreed, to a stay of proceedings awaiting the decision of the exchequer court.
Then this important paragraph follows:
Subsequently a settlement having been made with these companies, the appeals were withdrawn and as a result they were heard neither by the income tax appeal board nor by the exchequer court.
In the original return, I am informed by the same department, in all four cases the appeals were heard by the income tax appeal board, which ruled in favour of the company and then on appeal to the exchequer court that court ruled in favour of the government and reversed the decision of the appeal board. There, you have a discrepancy in the information and-

speechtext: It is quite customary to stay one action while another is being heard.

speechtext:
I am not quarrelling with what was done in that respect. I am pointing out that the information given in the first instance was not correct and does not agree with the information later given concerning two of those companies.
However, the remissions were made to these companies under the terms of the 50433-190
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny Financial Administration Act, section 22. In that section permission is given to the governor in council to make such remissions but there is a very important proviso to the effect that it must be in the public interest. The government is not permitted to just throw the public's money away any time they feel like it. They must justify that remission by proving it is in the public interest to do so.
In attempting to justify these remissions the Department of National Revenue stated two reasons in the original return. I quote:
Taking into consideration the uncertainty of the outcome of the pending appeals to the supreme court and of the effect of the new legislation, it was considered advisable to accept the offer of the settlement made by the company.
The appeal referred to is the one which two of the companies made to the supreme court after the exchequer court had ruled in favour of the government. The appeals were never heard but the actions were started. The effect of the new legislation referred to here is the fact that in 1953 the paragraph in section 12 to which I have referred earlier was repealed by section 4 of the amending act, so that subsequent to 1953 that paragraph no longer applied. But it is stated plainly in the amending act that the section is applicable to 1953 and subsequent taxation years.
In other words, that amendment had no legal effect whatsoever on the taxation years 1946 to 1952. And yet, let us examine these two reasons given to prove that it was in the public interest for the public treasury to hand back $2 million to these four companies, sums which they held in trust for Canada. One reason given was the uncertainty of the outcome of the pending appeals to the supreme court. That is a strange reason to give, in view of the fact that the exchequer court had ruled in favour of the government and stated their reasons for doing so. I have their judgment before me.
Surely, after having referred the matter to a court of proper jurisdiction, the government should have some confidence in the decision handed down by that court. There was no reason why there should have been any uncertainty as to the outcome of the appeal made on behalf of two of these companies. The other two did not even make their appeal to the supreme court. But the one that really strikes me as being strange indeed is the other reason in which it is said that the effect of the new legislation was considered. As I said, the new legislation was passed in 1953, and was to come into effect only for 1953 and subsequent years. It had nothing whatever to do with the case in dispute. If the legislation was valid constitutionally up to that time and was changed in
3002	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny
1953, then by its own laws the government was bound to proceed to collect taxes which under its own legislation became due.
Surely they would not introduce a principle that would leave the door open to any corporation in Canada to put pressure upon the government to change the Income Tax Act in its favour and then say, "Now that you have changed the act, let us go back to 1945 or 1944, and hand us back some of the taxes you took from us under previous legislation." In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was very careful to guard against that kind of thing when he said that certain provisions come into effect on July 1 or January 1, or that they would became effective immediately, as the case may be. None of these things is made retroactive, unless so stated. And it is stated here, plainly, that it is not retroactive, and that it is to take effect from 1953, on. So when one analyses the two reasons given he finds that neither is a valid one. And since neither is a valid reason there must have been others that are not stated. Certainly, in the light of the discrepancies in the return thus far, as time goes on I would not be surprised if we got a third answer. The situation is simply this: that, on the very weak pretence that the effect of amending the Income Tax Act in 1953 in some mysterious way had something to do with tax liability accrued from 1946 to 1952, and on the other flimsy ground that, owing to the uncertainty in the government's mind as to the outcome of the appeal to the supreme court, they felt that it was in the public interest to refund $2 million to these four corporations.
That is a very strange procedure, indeed. Because if the government proceeded by the proper methods, and if they felt that the treasury was entitled to the money they had received, they should have proceeded with the appeals to the supreme court and obtained a ruling in the matter. Then we would know where we stand. If they were not entitled to the money, then they should not have assessed it for liability.
As it now stands, the government has given a concession amounting to $2 million to four companies, and under circumstances which to me appear to be of a very suspicious nature. Until we have an explanation in the *house, and until we are told how the government can justify its action under section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, then we have every reason to continue to be suspicious and to believe that the Minister of Finance was rather optimistic when he congratulated the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) upon the efficient and impartial method used in collecting taxes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to stay away from that aspect of public affairs discussed by the hon. member who just sat down. Rather it is my intention today to discuss the guaranteed annual wage, the related problem of automation and the manner in which it may affect the economy of this country. Up to the present time the surface of the implication has scarcely been scratched; today I intend to do a little scratching at it. Most people ask, what is it all about? The workers say that if it is good for management to be paid by the year, then it is also good for the workers. The employers say it is illogical and uneconomic to pay wages to people who are not working.
I wish first to deal with automation. This is a new word used to describe the replacement of manpower by automatic machinery. Frequently this is described as the second industrial revolution, brought about by electronics. Let me place before the house a few examples of automation. The dial telephone is one; the machine in the telephone company which dials long distance calls, records the time and computes the cost is another; the electronic mail sorter is another. The machine in government offices which prints old age pensions and family allowances cheques by the thousands, and records them, is another; the machine that sends out premium notices from the large insurance companies is another. We are told that the Ford Motor Company has a new engine plant in Cleveland where six-cylinder engine blocks are turned out by an electronic brain which controls 42 automatic machine units. All that is done in 15 minutes. Formerly

it took nine hours to do that operation. The Toronto Star on April 19 carried a report from St. Catharines as follows:
The age of automation in Canada has been ushered in at a modern new plant of McKinnon Industries Limited, the one-time Canadian supplier to the saddle and buggy trade which now provides powerful engines for General Motors of Canada cars.
In the new plant in Grantham township near here, which was designed and built solely for the production of a new V-8 type of engine, mechanization has been advanced until a single operator monitoring panels of flashing lights can now control the continual flow of engine blocks through a 140-foot monster machine that performs hundreds of operations without the touch of a human hand.
There are many other instances, too many for me to mention here. As a result of those improvements no one is sure whether automation will merely jeopardize or destroy jobs. But one thing I think is certain, that automation will bring about some job dislocation which will require the shifting of workers to new jobs and to new employers. It is quite possible that if we find more ways to do more work in fewer man hours there will be more work to do, and thus it will increase employment. That of course has been the historic position of industry; we can go back to the time of the invention of the loom which could weave six webs at one time.
The workers are not fighting automation, but they want to cushion its effects and they want to share in its fruits. The guaranteed annual wage is the workers' concept of wiping out the insecurity of lay-offs and loss of wages. They look upon it as a challenge to management. Labour is asking management to guarantee to workers an annual wage in the same way management is now provided. They ask to share in the abundance. Labour does not ask that management subsidize idleness. They want less idleness; that is their chief complaint. They believe that the genius of management, under free enterprise, can help solve and destroy the evils of unemployment as they now resolve the problems of production and distribution. Nothing can be settled by ignoring this problem or by calling it names, so we might as well start discussing it.
The words "guaranteed annual wage" are something of a misnomer, since they do not quite mean what they say. Theoretically it could mean a guarantee of some wage for 52 weeks; practically it means a guarantee of some income or period of work. It has as its purpose two main objectives, the elimination of the short work week and the elimination of seasonal slack time lay-offs.
The arguments used by business today are the same ones that were advanced against the minimum wage law, workmen's 50433-190J
The Budget-Mr. Croll compensation, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, the eight-hour day and industrial pensions. The historic position of business has been that the guaranteed wage will bring on inflation, force bankruptcies and make workers lazy. We have heard all that before and it just did not happen. I ask this house whether all these improvements I have mentioned, and collective bargaining, holidays with pay and health benefits have harmed the economy or the people of this country.
My purpose in bringing this to the attention of the house is not to recommend a blind rush into guaranteed annual wage agreements. I do recommend to this house a very thorough examination. Job security and security of wage income have always been matters of great concern not only to the workers but to the employers, to the labour unions and to the governments. Thus guaranteed employment or wage plans have gained widespread support amongst wage earners, reflecting a very deep-rooted desire for steady jobs and steady incomes.
Let me be more explicit. A guaranteed employment, or a guaranteed wage plan, is a formal commitment by an employer to provide for all or some of his employees a stipulated amount of work or wages during the year. Under guaranteed employment a certain amount of work is guaranteed. Under the guaranteed wage plan income is guaranteed. The difference between the two forms is largely one of emphasis. Many employers have voluntarily attempted to provide year-round employment, not only because of such intangible but important benefits as better labour relations and the good will of the community, but also because of the savings to be derived from reduced turnover of personnel and the improved employee morale which result from eliminating the workers' fear of unemployment.
Employers in the main have been unwilling to commit themselves to guaranteed annual employment, fearing that seasonal or cyclical fluctuations, or both, may make fulfilment of that impossible. Some experts do say that stabilization of the workers' income, or lessening of the effect of unemployment, can be brought about to a certain extent through seniority rules, work sharing in slack seasons and dismissal pay.
These measures all help to bridge periods of unemployment or idleness. They do not provide security of income or employment. Seniority rules merely determine which employees are to be laid off. Sharing work also means sharing unemployment. Dismissal pay only softens the blow from the loss of

The Budget-Mr. Croll the job. Although unemployment insurance provides some income during slack periods, payments are comparatively small and continue for a short time. There is no doubt that unemployment insurance is helpful, but it is not a satisfactory substitute for regular and steady employment, and it was never intended to be that.
Let us for a few moments examine in a general way what are the implications of an annual wage guarantee. Of course many questions come to mind when considering a nation-wide application of a guaranteed annual wage. If we consider the feasibility of a guaranteed annual wage in the steel industry, and I use this only as an example, we are concerned immediately with the problem of synchronizing demand and employment with those of other interdependent industries.
Two questions undoubtedly arise in the minds of those who are giving this matter some thought. First, would the commitments of an individual firm under a general industry agreement for a guaranteed annual wage need to be reinforced from a more general pool of resources? The second question of course is whether such an undertaking would require government participation in the pool to take care of cases where a whole industry is in a depressed state.
Some of these questions may be answered by the fact that if a guaranteed annual wage plan were undertaken during present high employment, a fund of purchasing power in the hands of the consumer could be assured. This in turn would increase demand for new investment to match a sustained consumer market. The possibility of failure to meet commitments would thus be reduced to a minimum. Of course there is the further possibility that with the aid of unemployment insurance an annual wage program could become a reality.
It is axiomatic, and it has been so stated by many hon. members in the house, that where workers are assured of full employment and economic security they furnish a background for that mass of purchasing power so essential for the continued turning of the wheels of industry. The production of steel depends entirely upon the wheels of industry turning, which in turn depends upon both the purchasing power of the people at home and the demands of foreign markets. If the steel workers, and I again use them as an example, as a group are guaranteed an annual wage thereby assuring continuity of full employment, they have a stability which permits them to go out and purchase automobiles, refrigerators and the thousand and *one articles which require steel.

I intend to discuss for a few moments some of the arguments which have been presented from time to time in favour of an annual wage, and some which have been presented which are unfavourable to it. Let us examine the advantages of a guaranteed annual wage. The worker's feeling of security is increased; his morale is strengthened and maintained. Partially employed workers find it difficult to recognize the need for increased production when the results of their efforts are likely to result in lay-offs. Under a guaranteed wage the worker feels free to exert the maximum effort. He knows that increased effort on his part does not mean that he will lose his job.
Surveys indicate that many workers would prefer regular employment at moderate wages to irregular employment at high wages. Increased security would result in greater cooperation between labour and management. The worker's efficiency is likely to be improved. There will be less incentive to make work last. The sense of responsibility will be increased, resulting in less breakage and less faulty work.
The labour turnover may be reduced. Irregular employment often results in a high labour turnover, which increases costs because of the loss of trained men and the expense entailed in continually hiring new workers who have to be trained and whose initial efficiency may be low. The existence of an annual guaranteed wage plan will stimulate management to find ways and means to regularize production. Since workers will have to be paid whether or not there is work for them to do, every effort will be made by management to find something for them to do by trying to smooth out the variations in demand for the products of the industry and in the supply of its raw material, and by improving the organization of production and distribution.
To the extent that a guaranteed annual wage serves as a stimulus to the stabilization of production, unit overhead costs will be reduced because the same volume of production will be obtained with less capital, machinery and floor space, and a smaller labour force may well be needed. The stipulation that the guaranteed annual wage will not apply in certain specific instances might bring about a reduction in absenteeism, which would increase industrial output and thereby reduce costs. It is quite possible that there would be a beneficial effect on the economy as a whole. Other manufacturing industries and the retail trade would experience a greater stability of demand as a result of which consumption would be likely to be stimulated and investment in new undertakings encouraged.

Let us examine for a few moments some of the disadvantages which are from time to time put forward in opposition to a guaranteed annual wage. Those who are opposed say that if only a portion of the workers in a plant receive an annual wage the workers may be divided into two antagonistic groups resulting in a lower plant efficiency. The expense of operating a guaranteed wage plan may be greater than is justified by the benefits. This is particularly the case if work has to be done which involves increased variable as well as semi-variable costs. Greater stability may make it difficult for seasonal industries to acquire the temporary labour necessary to meet peak demands or to process raw materials available only at a particular season or time of the year.
The adoption of a guaranteed wage plan may force a firm to diversify its production, thereby increasing costs through a reduction of the economies which may be obtained from specialization. Further, a company may attempt to produce for stock when demand falls off, and this may prove to be a risky and costly undertaking which may outweigh any savings to be derived from operating at full capacity in a specialized industry. Business risks may be increased, and the entry of new firms may be discouraged.
A guarantee of wages would have the effect of converting some variable and semi-variable costs into fixed costs. This increased rigidity of the cost structure may make it difficult for a company to meet changing conditions successfully. The effect of this in any particular industry depends on the proportion which labour costs form of total costs. Another argument often heard is that it may have the effect of freezing the worker in his job and thus ending his mobility.
Those are some of the arguments pro and con which I have been able to marshal. There are many others. I felt the house was entitled to have both sides of the story now, since this will be a matter for discussion for some time yet.
I am going to be more specific now and deal with one particular problem. How would the guaranteed annual wage affect the automobile industry? Press reports indicate that it is now breathing down their neck. It is my own theory that the guaranteed annual wage is tailored for that industry and fits it like the paper on the wall. What is more, the industry by its very method of operation has been asking for it for a very long time. The constant and persistent lay-offs in that industry serve to spur the workers to obtain an income sufficient for 12 months. They and their families cannot be expected to go on
The Budget-Mr. Croll short rations from the day of the lay-off until the day the call to return to the assembly line is sounded.
No one denies that a corporation has a duty to its stockholders to see that its operations are efficiently run and make a profit, but there is another duty which must be harmonized with that responsibility for making profits. That is the duty to the men who make the profits possible, a clear recognition of their right to be freed from the spectre of constant and persistent lay-offs. By countenancing the valleys and peaks in their industry, they have indicated that the methods which in their fathers' day were best are not good enough today. These times demand new methods, new approaches and a clear grasp of what is right, proper and just.
The automobile industry operates under a high protective tariff which limits competition. It is controlled by the big three, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler, who take full advantage of the tariff. It is true that the industry has made great contributions to the economy and well-being of this country. They pay good wages, but for too short a time. High wages are not a substitute for employment.
It must also be said that the industry has grown in importance and influence, and in the process has become rich in business and fat in profits. It is about time the rules were revised, because the industry has turned a bad habit into a practice, by producing at a very high rate for nine or ten months and then turning the workmen out to fend for themselves or become a charge upon the municipality until they are once again needed. With the advent of unemployment insurance workers collect benefits during unemployment, but these are still much less than normal pay. They now ask that work be spaced so they can work regularly in order that they may eat regularly.
The pattern of the industry is about as follows. They have six months of concentrated production, followed by four months of normal production which tapers off to a trickle, and then a two-months' lay-off. This is usually done under the guise of stocktaking, retooling for new models, renovating, repairing and maintenance, which is done with minute and tender care for the plant and the machinery. During that period the workers must look out for themselves; there is no maintenance for the workers as such.
The record of the industry is very interesting. During the years 1924 to 1928 the employment variation in the industry was 27'4 per cent. During the years 1947 to 1951 the employment variation was 4-7 per cent-

speechtext:
I said that the variation between 1924 and 1928 was 27-4 per cent. The variation in employment from 1947 to 1951 was 4-7 per cent. Now, once again the industry is being subjected to sharp short-term lay-offs which are increasing in number and severity. In the face of competition the employment variation now is almost three times what it was in the 1947-1951 period. It is rising again. Thus by the failure of the industry to correct the pattern which I have indicated, it has for the present time lost the initiative by default.
I do not think the guaranteed annual wage will affect industry adversely. I think it will provide it with an exercise in planning and economics which it can solve in the same way it has solved other very difficult problems. If they must find work for their employees on a year-round basis they will learn to make cuckoo clocks, and they will make them better than anybody has made them before. They will sell more and more, and sell them on the time payment plan in order to provide employment and profit. It is not good enough for industry to say that they have to meet consumer demand, for it is well known that they not only stimulate but they create consumer demand.
It must be said in fairness to them that industry is not unaware of its shortcomings and has attempted to meet the situation by bringing out new models in the fall rather than in the spring, and thus have a winter selling season. That is a laudable effort to stabilize the industry, but in the face of competition they are reverting to the old practice and the old pattern once again, and that is a dangerous one. The industry-and I think I know it well-is fortunate in that it has not only genius but talent within its ranks. The genius has been devoted to engineering, mechanization, production, distribution and automation; the talent to the human problems, the workers and labour relations. That is not good enough. It is time they applied the genius where they now apply the talent.
The guaranteed annual wage is not revolutionary; it seems to me rather evolutionary.
I believe that the companies are hungry for a solution, but are fearful of breaking new ground and fearful of letting the team down. They can meet the challenge if the big three will undertake to do it collectively. Here is a great opportunity for them to give leadership by doing away with these periodic and 

what appear to be totally unnecessary layoffs. The guaranteed annual wage has been operated chiefly in the United States, where only a small portion of the workers have been covered, and the same thing is true of Canada.
In replying to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on February 14, the Minister of Labour said in effect that no study was being made by the department of the guaranteed annual wage. In answering the question he also had something further to say. He said that in 1953 there were two guaranteed annual wage plans in manufacturing industries in Canada and three guaranteed annual plans in nonmanufacturing industries, the total number of employees covered being 1,900. One plan has since been discontinued.
In 1954 there were eight guaranteed annual wage plans with a total number of employees of something like 1,050. To bring the house up to date, my information is that in 1955 we must add to that number the John Labatt Company of London which employs 500, the Pert Hosiery company of Montreal which employs 60, and the Eaton Knitting Company of Hamilton which employs 150. Some other countries have recently introduced guaranteed wage plans, but they have generally restricted them to a certain limited number of hours of work per week.
My purpose in rising today was to anticipate a measure such as this which can have a healthy effect upon our economy. Just as many of us have envisaged and fought for measures of social and labour betterment, minimum wages, workmen's compensation, the eight-hour day and 40-hour week, unemployment insurance and so on, so we have to give thought now to the guaranteed annual wage. While we have a high level of employment at the present time, we must maintain that condition by all the devices at our disposal. I do not regard the guarantee of wages as a panacea, but I do think it is a tool which can be put to work to round out a program of greater security, and which will make for harmonious industrial relations and a more lasting prosperity. At least we can give some study to advance the frontiers of knowledge in this particular field. This would give us a chance to bone up in order to create a climate of understanding and informed opinion with respect to what appears on the horizon.
Before the great debate, which may give off more heat than light, becomes one of great contention, we should give it study. In the light of the minister's answer to the hon. member, to which I have already

alluded, it is my suggestion that the department make a careful and minute study of the implications of the guaranteed annual wage, and when it is completed turn over the report to the committee of this house on industrial relations for study and understanding. That would have the beneficial effect of creating a more thorough understanding by members of the House of Commons and the country generally.
This is no time to stand aloof. It will be on us before we know it. I think we should study the problem before it becomes a labour issue. In that light I present the matter to the government for consideration.

Mr. Speaker, in examining the budget I think we must look first to see what is in it and, second, find out, if we can, why this particular budget was presented. First of all I am going to examine the budget and then a little latter I shall describe why I think it was presented.
In examining the budget, may I say that I think it has failed in the main purpose of a budget brought down in a period like this, which should be to provide the stimulus necessary to restore the pace of industrial production, trade and employment.
The first point is the reduction in the income tax. It amounts to 27 cents a week for a married man with two children earning $3,000 a year, which is considerably above the average for Canada. It amounts to 50 cents a week for a married man with two children earning $5,000 a year. That kind of tax reduction is not going to give anybody the incentive to go out and buy a television set, a washing machine, a refrigerator, a stove, a suit of clothes, or any of the things produced by the industries that are hardest hit today. It is going to create very little stimulus to sales in those industries, and I think it has failed in that regard.
The 2 per cent reduction in corporation tax was welcomed by industry but, Mr. Speaker, how much of that 2 per cent is going to be passed on to the consumers in the form of lower prices aimed at stimulating sales? I think very little. It will also do very little to stimulate plant expansion, because it will merely mean a saving of $10,000 to a company earning a profit of $500,000 before taxes. That is not enough to cause most companies to embark on a capital expansion program.
The third thing the budget did was to introduce a 5 per cent reduction in the excise tax on new cars. What does that amount to? It amounts to a saving of $75 on a new popular priced car. But the great majority of Canadians buy new cars on time, and the
The Budget-Mr. Hees great obstacle in their path is the down payment. Therefore the 5 per cent reduction is not going to help them very much.
Although the budget has undoubted political appeal, it does not do the job required of a budget brought down in a period of economic slow-down, such as we are experiencing today. It is a superficial budget, aimed at taking people's minds away from the fact that the government has no plan for counteracting our basic economic ills.
By the announcement of the appointment of a royal commission to study our economy the government has recognized the need for such a plan. But I want to ask the government this question. What has it been doing in the ten years that have intervened between 1945 and now, since the introduction of the famous white paper in 1945 which recognized this need? During those ten years the various departments of the government should have been collecting the kind of information which the royal commission will collect in the next few years. The royal commission will require several years to collect the information, and several more years will probably be required then before the government gets around to formulating an economic plan.
If the government had had its various departments gathering the information which the royal commission will now gather, a plan for industrial expansion could have been put into operation some time ago, and we would not be experiencing the economic slow-down which we are experiencing today. For 15 years the government has been content to ride the crest of an economic boom which it was convinced would never end, but it did end in this past year. Now they have suddenly come to realize that this country is facing economic problems for which they have no answers. In desperation they have turned to the appointment of a royal commission to do the job they should have been doing for the past ten years. The problems we are up against today, Mr. Speaker, are simply the problems which were bound to present themselves when the nations devastated by war got on their feet, and when countries like the United States started looking around aggressively for markets into which to dump their surplus production. They certainly found one in Canada.
So today, Mr. Speaker, this government is trying to cover up its incompetence by turning to the device of appointing a royal commission to obtain information which they should have been collecting during the past ten years. There is no excuse for them not having obtained that information. They recognized the need in the white paper of 1945, and then went completely asleep and did

The Budget-Mr. Hees nothing about it. The government realize they have no information upon which to formulate an economic plan, and the country is taking the rap.
I suppose that in the meantime, until this royal commission reports, this government is going to be quite content to sit back and do nothing. During the next four years, while this investigation is under way, the government will pursue its usual policy of hope and grope, somehow expecting that something is going to turn up-the something that just does not seem to turn up. I do not believe the average Canadian considers that kind of approach good enough. This government is caught badly off base, and it is making no attempt to do anything about it except admit it has no information on which to formulate a plan, and admit it is not going to do anything until this royal commission reports. The government knows quite well it will be several years before the commission can report. I think this is a disgraceful situation for any government to have to admit, but this government is admitting it today because it has no alternative.
Now, although the government cannot come up with any suggestions or any plan, and even though this government is too autocratic, too dictatorial, too self-satisfied to ever accept suggestions from the opposition, it is still our responsibility, failing any suggestions from the government side, to make suggestions concerning what we feel has to be done to pull our economy out of the doldrums in which it finds itself today.
I am going to make a few suggestions. I think what we must do first is try to formulate a plan which will start industrial expansion in this country and will provide steadily increasing employment, a steadily increasing standard of living. That is the only positive approach to this problem of unemployment and lost markets which this government is doing nothing to meet. To do this I believe we must achieve two important aims. The first is to improve the design and lower the cost of the products we manufacture. It is only by so doing that we can protect and improve our competitive position against the products which are made outside of Canada, and which are giving us such severe competition today.
Second, I believe we must greatly expand our secondary industries within this country so we can process a far greater proportion of our primary products than we are doing today. When we do that we will provide jobs for Canadians instead of simply providing the raw materials with which workmen in other countries will turn out finished materials, many of which we buy back.


The steps which I believe we must take to accomplish these objectives are five in number and I should like to deal with each in turn. First, in order to develop new and better designs and more efficient methods of production, we must undertake a greatly expanded program of industrial research, based on the programs which have proved so effective in Great Britain, the United States, Germany and several industrial countries in Europe. Unless our efforts in this regard can match theirs at least on a per capita basis, then we must expect to have their products continue to beat ours in price or design or both. Such a program, Mr. Speaker, has made it possible for Great Britain to announce, on the same day we announced our highest unemployment figure here, their second lowest. Under that program Great Britain's unemployment has continued to decrease and ours has continued to grow. I feel that is a rather astonishing state of affairs for this country to have to admit.
Now, what is needed to achieve that end is for the government to call a conference of the representatives of management, labour and the educational institutions, who will produce most of the research staff, to discuss the best methods for getting a program of this kind under way. Such a program would include the pooling of technical information to be used by those engaged in an industry to compete, as an industry, against foreign competition. I believe that only by so doing can we compete successfully against the competition which we are receiving from other countries, and which gives every indication of continuing to increase rather than to decrease.
Second, I believe that in order to expand our secondary industries we must take steps which will make it attractive for new industries to become established and for existing industries to expand. I think we must remember that this is a free country, and unless conditions are sufficiently attractive to invite the expansion of established industries they are not going to expand, and new industries are simply not going to become established. One step I think we should take in this direction is to double the rate of depreciation on plant and equipment, and by so doing reduce the risks to those investing in new enterprise. Spread over the original depreciation period this move will cost the government absolutely nothing.
Another step I think we should take to encourage new industries to become established is to make it easier for them to show their first net profit. I believe a move we could make in this direction would be to

reduce the rate of taxation on small businesses from the present 18 per cent to 15 per cent, and raise the ceiling from $20,000 to $25,000. I believe that in addition to this, in order to encourage these small industries to expand into large industries consideration should be given to the advantages of increasing the tax at a steady rate from the top of the lowest tax bracket up to a profit of say $50,000 a year before taxes. I think the sudden jump from the present 18 per cent on up to $20,000 to 47 per cent on the next $1,000 of profit is a deterrent to expansion today. I feel the government should give serious consideration to a steady increase in the rate of taxation rather than a sudden jump. If that were done it would give small industries, at present established and remaining small, an incentive to expand into large industries of the kind we need.
While the move I have suggested, of reducing the corporation tax, would reduce the income from that source for the time being, I believe the additional taxes which would accrue in the future from new enterprises which would be encouraged to start up and expand with the aid of this move and double depreciation would very soon, in my opinion, make up any deficit.
