A third move I believe the government should make to stimulate sales is to reduce the sales tax by 25 per cent. This would greatly reduce the cost of things we have to sell and would place our products in a far better competitive position as against those from other countries competing with them today. It would be an important stimulus to sales, because it would make it possible for those in the lower income groups to buy more goods, and after all, they are the ones who are in greatest need of such goods and who will be most ready to buy. They are the ones who are hardest hit by the tax, because it is a tax which is applied without any consideration for ability to pay.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The fourth move I suggest the government should make to stimulate our trade is that of bringing the value of the Canadian dollar down to parity with the United States dollar. This would make it more attractive for people from outside to buy Canadian goods, and would attract more tourists to this country.
As I have said, I believe these tax reductions would only temporarily reduce total tax receipts. A temporary deficit in my opinion would be well worth while if, by so doing, trade were stimulated and there was a stimulation of production to the point where in the near future it would be greater than it is at the present time. This would increase the tax totals the government would receive, because it would increase greatly the sources from which taxes come. I believe the minister will agree that, after all, that is the desirable end.
If in the meantime the government did make an all-out effort to streamline its operations, something it has made no effort to do up to this time, the savings which could be brought about in government operations would more than offset any temporary deficit which would be caused by tax reductions. In the long run I believe the moves I have suggested would substantially increase our tax revenue by increasing the sources from which taxes come, and for that reason I say these moves should be given serious consideration by the government.
In conclusion let me say that because the government has been lethargic in the past ten years and has collected no information upon which to base an economic plan, the establishment of a royal commission is a very necessary move indeed. In the meantime there is a big job to be done in facing the severe competition we are up against right now, a condition the government is making no attempt whatever to meet. Upon our success or failure in meeting that competition depend the jobs of our workmen and the standard of living of our people. I believe the steps I have suggested would help materially in meeting this challenge, and I urge the government to give these matters serious consideration.
As I said earlier, it is interesting to diagnose what has been the purpose of the government in producing a budget of this kind. It is certainly clear to me that the budget does nothing to stimulate sales or production, so why was it brought in? I think those of us

The Budget-Mr. Hees who gathered here on the night of April 5 to hear the budget speech were rather surprised, when finally we had a look at the baby, to see that it had draped over its shoulder a banner upon which were written the words, "Liberal convention, 1956; vote for Walter Harris". And if there was any doubt in anyone's mind that that was the purpose of the budget, that indeed it was a convention budget, all he had to do was to look at the faces of the other six hopefuls. Each of them, Mr. Speaker, looked like a man who had just received news that his mother in law was coming to spend six weeks with him.
The one who really looked as though he was suffering most was fisherman Jack from Twillingate. He was really suffering. I thought he was choking on a piece of herring bait. He looked as though his rubber boots were a couple of sizes too small, and he actually felt so badly that he had to pull his sou'wester halfway down his face, during the speech, to hide the tears running down his cheeks.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no doubt in my mind that this is the first move in the campaign to build up an Uncle Walter myth. Because after all, Mr. Speaker, it is understandable that this should be done, particularly when the minister has seen what success the boss has met with in the last seven years in handing out this kind of malarkey.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Envy will get you nowhere. You are the malarkey man in the house right now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How is your campaign coming on?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister said to himself, no doubt, "If it works for him, why should it not work for me?" So he set himself the task of schooling himself to fill this particular role. And, Mr. Speaker, those of us who have observed the minister closely in the last couple of weeks have noticed that very often he has had a sort of dreamy, far-away look in his eye, the look of a man who sees thousands of little children gathered at whistle stops all across the country. As he walks down the corridor you often notice him now- you people in the House of Commons just watch him and see if this is not true-no doubt it is quite unconscious, but you can see the movement of his hands as he walks along the corridors, patting countless little tousled heads as he walks through the crowds and hands out the soothing syrup to the mothers of babies. Yes, the minister is working very 

hard at this, and more power to him. It worked for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and no doubt the Minister of Finance has set his sights on the job.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You certainly tried to make it work from coast to coast last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has not got away with it in the past, because the minister of citizenship and propagation, of course, has said himself that babies are his business. He is not going to let the Minister of Finance muscle in on his racket. So what did he do? As soon as the blow fell on the night of April 5 he went out and arranged for one of those new private cars the government sends around the country with its ministers, and he did not take just an ordinary trip. He took a real trip away across the country out to Victoria to make a political speech. And did he make a political speech? Out there he told the mothers of the country that they must produce more babies for him to pat. He is coming around and he wants to have them there, and he wants to be able to pat them.
After all, you cannot blame him for not taking this thing lying down, because this minister was told by the Prime Minister, when he was brought out of the back room and set so uncomfortably on the front bench, that he was the heir apparent. He does not like this kind of a budget being brought in by the Minister of Finance because it is a direct threat to him, and he is not taking it. Therefore he went out and made a speech. It was not a bad speech either, Mr. Chairman; it was fine, except that he made the great mistake of antagonizing every Canadian citizen who did not happen to be born in Canada. He told them in effect that they are second-class citizens and that they can never acquire the status of those of us who were fortunate enough to be born in Canada.
It is amazing to me how a minister who has his foot in his mouth for 95 per cent of the time can manage to make so many political speeches. It seems to me the only answer is that he is a contortionist and is able to do it. It is amazing that every time he makes a speech he pulls off one of those masterpieces. I do not know how he does it, but he certainly does it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us get back to the budget. It was not produced without a lot of trouble. During the nine-month gestation period, which lasted from the time the minister was promoted early in July until early in April, there were several very anxious moments. One of them came at the four-

months' point. It was a very critical time in Montreal, last November, and for a while it looked as though there had been a premature birth, but the minister straightened that out and everything was all set. Then the seven-months' stage was reached, and his old department came up for scrutiny. Normally he would be expected to be on hand to defend his old department, but the government felt that would be a little too trying at this particular time, so they called in the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) to take on those noble knights, Sir John of Prince Albert and Sir Davie of Kamloops. The hon. member did very well, but of course he was no match for the two great debaters and they demolished him.

speechtext: Pretty weak at this moment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To use a fisheries expression, he is floundering.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It all adds up to the fact that
this is obviously a convention budget, Mr. Speaker, one that is intended, as I see it, to build up the minister as a successor to the Prime Minister. The objective is to build up an Uncle Walter myth in the same way they built up the Uncle Louis myth, and that is about all it is accomplishing.
In the meantime the country is forced to suffer. There are no economic plans; there is nothing to stimulate production; there is nothing to stimulate sales, and there is no indication that there is to be any plan from the government for at least three or four years, or until the royal commission reports. In the meantime the country is going to be left to flounder. We are going through the same process of hope and grope, and to me it is a sad commentary on a government to bring in a budget at this time with no indication of any plan to overcome any of our economic ills. All they can do is to appoint a royal commission to do something which they know perfectly well they should have been doing for the past ten years and have simply failed to do. The country and the people have to take the rap for this government's lethargy, and that is about the saddest commentary one can make on any government's budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join the great majority of Canadians who, through the newspapers of this country, have expressed their approval and satisfaction about the budget recently submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).
50433-191*
The Budget-Mr. Roy
When the budget was brought down last year, we were urged to be hopeful, and we have not been deceived because this year we are feeling the good results.
True, there is nothing to make us hysterical, but it is a first step which has started the wheel turning and we have reason to believe in the enthusiastic optimism of the Minister of Finance, who assures us that the wheel will keep on turning, and that every future budget will bring a gradual lowering of taxes, for the greatest benefit of the various classes of Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, the economic situation of the country has been fraught for the past few months with thorny problems which, from certain points of view, have a tendency to upset the sustained equilibrium that has been enjoyed these past years. That is why, more than ever, business activity must be held at a stable level, and in order to prevent economic stagnation or a serious recession, the government must take the necessary means to preserve this stability which has been the basis of our prosperity in the last fifteen years.
Particularly in the last ten years, the government has remained faithful to a policy of gearing expenditures to the economic situation. We had come to believe that it was necessary to ensure budgetary surpluses and, on no account, to accept deficits. It is only at this time that we are realizing the wisdom of the present government which has been adhering to the principle that surpluses must be accumulated in times of prosperity, the longterm view being that we must be prepared to sustain a deficit without too much trouble should national interest so require, in order to ensure the soundness of our economy.
The Canadian people have approved this policy of accumulating surpluses in order to improve our position in case we have to resort to deficit financing and have judged it a wise and farsighted policy. Our budget accounts show that, last year, Canada had started a gradual climb toward a more rational economic stability. Past records indicate that the figures pertaining to the gross national product, employment, income, manpower and economic trends in most sectors of our economy seemed to stabilize at a slightly lower level, when they did not decline.
These facts moved the government, in order to curb any tendency toward a radical and highly dangerous recession, to use the accumulated reserves for the purpose of

The Budget-Mr. Roy
maintaining stability and preventing everywhere any overly unfavourable effects. We are beginning to notice that we are entering a period of readaptation which may entail some slight changes in the level of our economic activity. Taking heed of these indications, the government has shown in the budget its readiness to take the necessary steps and the people of Canada are happy to see the foresight of the present administration. The government did not remain idle, did not count only on the hope of a probable business pick-up on a world-wide scale. On the contrary, it went to work and made concessions to individual and corporate taxpayers. It is about to allocate more money for public works, to make it easier for people to get credit in order to speed up home building. It has seen to it that the seaway works are carried out without delay, that the buying power is increased through higher unemployment insurance benefits, quite apart from the numerous other moves it has made to stimulate employment and to maintain a sound business activity.
That is why the Canadian people were very pleased with the last budget. The Minister of Finance has gained the esteem of all Canadians, who are praising his remarkable financial talent and his deep understanding of our Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my constituents, I wish to sincerely thank the government for certain generous moves it has made:
First of all, the continuation for another year of price support for butter gives respite to most of my farmer constituents. In my district, more than in any other, there is an urgent need for such price support, because the dairy industry is in a less favourable position than elsewhere in the province, due to various factors peculiar to that district.
As a matter of fact, production is limited, both in its intensity and variety, by insufficient means of production, and the volume of any particular product seldom reaches a high enough level to be marketed at a profit. Therefore, as the farmer in my constituency is unable both to produce and to dispose of his production as economically as most farmers in other districts of the province, and, besides, as he has to face market fluctuations with prices falling sometimes below basic price, he finds it hard to make ends meet, when he does not suffer a loss.
Dairying accounts for 85 per cent of farm production in my county and with such an uncertain revenue, our farmers are obliged to ask the government to stabilize the industry by preventing the importation

into the country of vegetable oils for the manufacture of margarine, which competes unfairly with butter on the market.
I might, moreover, recommend to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) a substantial increase in the subsidies for the transport of grain to our district, so as to allow the farmers to stabilize their production cost at the same level as in the other districts of the province.
I associate myself with the hon. members from New Brunswick in supporting their request to the government of price support on potatoes, for this is an important industry in my county, and introducing such a measure would be a valuable contribution to the stability of farm revenues in that district.
Mr. Speaker, income from the agricultural industry provides a livelihood for 10 per cent at the most of the farmers in my district. To supplement their income and balance their budget, they have to work in the lumber industry. In this case, our farmers are deprived of a reasonable income because of the unfair practices of the buying companies that collude to purchase wood from farmers at ridiculous prices. I am happy to have cooperated with my colleague, the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc), in bringing about the federal inquiry now being made. I hope the provincial government will co-operate sincerely to compel the guilty companies to pay reasonable prices to our farmers and settlers for the wood purchased from them.
In addition to being forced to sell their wood at a loss, our farmers find their wood-lots being practically depleted. They are thus deprived of a necessary source of income. The leaders of our farm industry are anxious to see our governments take the urgent steps necessary to cope with this problem, which is of vital importance for our farmers. I will therefore make so bold as to suggest to the government that it should put this very important question on the agenda of the next federal-provincial conference. Of vital interest to our farmers and colonists is this matter of reforestation of their lands in co-operation with the province. Already many farmers are quitting the land because of the loss of revenue caused by this depletion of their woodlots. A survey carried out by agricultural officials has shown that a very large percentage of the total farming population will follow suit in the next ten years. I urge the government to give this matter its most earnest consideration. The solution of this problem is highly important.

One last suggestion, Mr. Speaker. The government should do away with middlemen in the contacts between Central Mortgage and Housing and the home builder. Since the state would appear to maintain and increase its guarantees in the home-building field, it would seem only fair for it to ensure that the credit it extends be as inexpensive and as easy as possible to obtain throughout this country. Many contractors have complained to me that banks and other lending institutions show little inclination to lend money in connection with buildings erected away from heavily populated centres. That gap should be filled in the best interests of the many people who wish to build a home.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I commend the government for its decision to grant a pension to disabled people. The citizens of Canada deeply appreciate such a move, which constitutes one more step toward social security.
This year again, I wish to convey the general opinion of the people of Canada that the government should now implement a health insurance plan in Canada. This useful step would relieve the constant pressure towards an increase of family allowances, would complete the social security legislation of the country, would maintain the economic effects of family allowances, whose value has been reduced to less than half their former worth, and, through a higher level of health among the people, would contribute to the establishment of a strong, spirited and productive nation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address this large and enthusiastic house this afternoon I feel greatly inspired. It is so quiet that it is more like a cathedral. I listened with a great deal of interest this afternoon to the discourse by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) on the guaranteed annual wage. I compliment him upon the presentation he made. It was a good speech, and it enabled him to avoid talking about the budget. Therefore his speech served two purposes. However, as I say, he did make a good speech on that subject and I am not going to repeat it.
I mention it merely because the potential leader of the opposition, according to the press, who followed him in the debate failed to make any comment on this matter of a guaranteed annual minimum wage, which is a most important subject at this time to organized labour on the North American
The Budget-Mr. Gillis continent. He may have been so preoccupied with his notes that he missed making any observation on this most important question.
If one sits here for two or three days and listens to the speeches made in most debates, one begins to wonder what is the subject matter before the house. I try to be realistic; I generally try to talk on the subject under discussion. As I understand it, the subject before the house at the present time is the budget presented by the Minister of Finance in a very well considered and excellently delivered speech. Many proposals are contained in that budget speech, tax relief to the income taxpayer, relief for corporations, and so forth.
Nov;, I am not going to take the budget and make any analysis of it, because I do not have to. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who is the chief spokesman for this group, in consultation with all other members of the group has done a first-class job in analysing the budget in all its aspects. He raked it over and turned, it over and made an excellent presentation,, and I agree with everything he had to say-on the budget as such.
In addition to the budget, with its many proposals, there is an amendment moved by the Conservative party, the official opposition. I am going to put it on the record again, because I am going to talk about these amendments in their relationship to the budget. The official opposition spokesman, at page 2954, in moving his amendment, worded it as follows:
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in its budget proposals the government has failed:
(a)	to give effective stimulus to Canadian enterprise to create employment and opportunity;
(b)	to reduce taxation affecting those on lower incomes and allowances;
(c)	to curb its own extravagance and inefficiency;
(d)	to recognize the serious position in which the Canadian farmer and other producers now find themselves".
The leader of this group, at page 2958, moved that this amendment be amended byadding at the end thereof the following words:
"(e) to provide assistance to the provincial governments, in order to enable them to plan their financing in such a manner as to relieve the people of this country from the crushing load of heavy municipal taxation."
Now, I want to make it quite clear, in so far as the budget is concerned, that all the economic, social and financial problems of this country today are not the product of the government as such. They are the product of a system, and the government which is in

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
power has to play the rules of the game as they are laid down. While the official opposition makes speeches and criticizes the party in power, in my judgment after sitting in this house for some considerable time there is only one motive for that criticism. There is never any suggestion as to what they could do themselves to change the system to bring relief and alleviation for the economic and social problems which are a product of this system and not the product of the government as such.
In their amendment I see nothing by way of a program, a policy or a criticism that would change the situation one iota. Asking the government to curb their own inefficiency and that kind of thing does not mean anything. In the face of a bad unemployment situation, all it means to me is that you should fire a lot of people who are now employed by the government, but that adds to the unemployment problem. There is nothing in their amendment that suggests that they would do anything different from what the government is doing at the present time. In fact they could not do anything. If they are going to follow strictly the lines of free enterprise as administered today by those outside of this house who control the economy, they could not do anything other than what is being done over there at the present time. Someone has to get on that side of the house who believes in taking the courageous stand of retaining what is good in the system of the past and purging it of the things that are evil; and I do not see the official opposition taking that stand, either in their amendment or in their speeches in this house.
The amendment of the C.C.F. party is merely tacked on. The rules of the house prevent us from laying down the kind of amendment we would like to move. We merely add that the government should take some action in regard to assistance to provincial governments whereby those governments may be in a position to relieve the heavy burden of municipal taxes which are charged against property exclusively. Property in the municipalities across Canada today is taxed to the hilt; it cannot go any higher.
It is at the lower level that assistance is needed. I do not say that it should be uniform or could be uniform. Some of the provinces, such as Ontario and Quebec and maybe British Columbia, which have large provincial incomes, are in a better position to help the municipalities-and they are doing so in many cases-than other provinces I know of, such as the maritimes and to some extent the prairie provinces, where they are not able to achieve uniformity in education IMr. Gillis.]

and many other things provided in the provinces which have incomes enabling them to do such things.
I think that is one of the most important matters for the federal government to consider. I know a dominion-provincial conference is being held shortly, and there is no doubt that will be part of the agenda. There is a need today particularly to take care of the employable unemployed. While we have revised unemployment insurance, and it helps those who are receiving unemployment insurance, thousands of men who have run off the unemployment insurance rolls are now considered as charges on the municipal governments, who are unable to do anything for them. That is a question which has to be handled, and handled soon.
With respect to the budget itself, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has, I think, pointed up two very important questions which should be considered by the Minister of Finance and his advisers. I agree with him that the proper place to give relief, in so far as income tax is concerned, was the lower income groups. Increasing the exemptions rather than cutting taxes at this time was the line of action the minister should have taken. The exemptions should have been lifted high enough so that married people on $3,000 income and single people on $1,500 income would be taken out of the income tax brackets altogether. If you are going to put purchasing power in the hands of the people of this country so they can buy and help break the jam of unemployment, then these are the groups to which that relief should have been handed out, because the people in those income brackets are the people who spend about 90 per cent of their income on fuel, clothing, shelter and food.
As to the people earning over $3,000, it would not matter to me if the minister had increased the rates. It is not what you pay in taxes that counts but what you have left after you have paid the taxes. I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was absolutely right when he suggested that is what the minister should have done in order to make up for the revenue he would lose by granting income tax exemption to the people in the low income brackets up to the level I have mentioned.
In the time at my disposal this afternoon I am going to talk about economic matters, but before I do so may I say that in listening to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) I was at a loss to understand his logic in his criticism of the budget. First he set out to prove that the budget was no good, that it was

a bad budget, offered no relief and did nothing for anybody. Then in the next breath he said it was a convention budget, a budget to build up the Minister of Finance as the next prime minister.
If it is a bad budget it is not going to do the Minister of Finance any good, or enhance his popularity at the convention. The hon. member for Broadview cannot have it both ways. First he says it is no good; then he says it is a good budget and is going to make the Minister of Finance the next prime minister. As far as I am concerned he has to straighten out his logic on that point to prove to me that he actually was criticizing the budget honestly, because his afterthought was that it was an excellent budget and was going to build up the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a Progressive Conservative. He goes both ways.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, you could perhaps have a worse prime minister than the present Minister of Finance. We know him pretty well. You see, Mr. Speaker, I am never particularly anxious to throw someone out of a job in order to get it myself, and I have not seen very much of a threat from the official opposition in the time I have been in the house or anything to indicate that they would bring about any great improvement if they were on the other side. It is better to hang on to the fellow you know who is at least trying to do a little bit than the fellow who just wants to get over there for the purpose of being on the front benches and being called a minister.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Broadview.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the present condition of the country and the international situation call for more serious thought than that. Of course we are fortunate because during war we are always very lucky. We have a lot of sensible privates who win the war despite the generals, and the same thing applies to governments. I think we underestimate the intelligence of the people in making their selection of those who are to represent them in the House of Commons. I believe we can pretty well depend on their judgment to do things right. That is why I am reasonably sure the C.C.F. is going to be pretty close to the government after the next federal election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You
are pretty close to the government right now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At least there would be this much improvement. We tell you in the house
The Budget-Mr. Gillis what we would do. We do not take the position in the house of hammering at the government for a lot of things they are not doing, knowing at the same time that if we were over there we would take exactly the same position. That is what the Progressive Conservatives would do but they would be a little worse than the present government. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: God forbid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we were over there now we would have stepped up the exemptions and we would have increased the taxes of the fellow who has the money. We would have got a lot of money by imposing a capital gains tax on the coupon clippers, described so well by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who can have an increase of $10,000 or $15,000 a year from the stock market without paying a cent of income tax on it. That is a nice exemption. We would have done something like that.
There is another thing we would have done. We would have been a little tougher on these fellows from outside the country who virtually have control of our economy through leases and so forth. We would see that their business was conducted along a little more honest lines than it is today. There would not be the same manipulation. We would not be selling the country down the river by admitting United States capital and giving these fellows leases for the next thousand years on the resources of the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who would you get to
develop them?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who would you get to develop them? That is a very courageous question, isn't it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take them over.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You would not have to take them over. You would finance and develop them in the same way we fought and financed the last war. We did not have to go outside the country to borrow money. The Bank of Canada was designed to do that very thing. Where private enterprise fell down the government could institute a public investment program and develop the resources of the country, just as little Joey Smallwood is doing today in Newfoundland.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are talking like your friends to your left.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I am not. That was Mackenzie King's idea. He practically told us when the Bank of Canada was established

The Budget-Mr. Gillis that he who controls the credit and currency of the country controls the country, and that the Bank of Canada was being established so the government would have some control over currency and credit in the event of Canada having to develop its own resources. We should never have sold our iron ore deposits and the future of steel down the river for the rest of our natural lives to a few monopolists in the United States. But that is what we did, and I did not notice very much opposition from the official opposition. The only opposition came from this corner.
We could have developed those resources ourselves. We could have farmed them out, held 51 per cent of the shares in the right of the Canadian people and given free enterprise the opportunity to get in on it if it wanted to do so. We could make it a partnership deal, but why sell out 100 per cent and lose control of the future of steel on the North American continent? That is exactly what it meant.
I want to say something about what is going on today in the maritime provinces. Economic conditions in that part of the country are anything but good. In making his speech the Minister of Finance stated that he was taking a gamble at this time. He said he was budgeting for a deficit in the face of a 2 per cent drop in our gross national product for the past year, but in taking that gamble he figured that the gross national product was going to increase this year by maybe 5 or 6 per cent. I hope it will, but I can tell him that if he is expecting any of that increase to take place in the maritime provinces he is going to be disappointed. The economic trend in that part of Canada today is just the reverse. Established industries that were producing in 1954 are not producing today.
Let me deal with the question of coal mining. That, of course, is the basic industry of the province of Nova Scotia, and to some extent it was a substantial industry in New Brunswick. The provincial government of Nova Scotia hired an outstanding firm in the United States to make a survey of their whole economic set-up. They recommended a lot of things, but they pinpointed the fact that in Nova Scotia the coal industry was the base of the economy. They pointed out it was in difficulties at the present time and that a lot of things had to be done if it were going to survive.
If Canada was a country that was exporting coal, if we had a big outside market, were producing a lot of coal and were not importing any, I would say that if there were any difficulties the cause would perhaps be faulty development and the fact that the mines were


not operating properly, but in a country like Canada that could not be so because at the present time we are importing around 24 million tons each year from the United States. A large percentage of that is imported by the Canadian National Bailways. We only produce around 16 or 17 million tons of coal ourselves. On many occasions in this house I have asked why a country that is importing that amount of coal should have no market for its own coal. I have never got an answer to that.
It is the same old story. In the area represented by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McCulloch) in the last four years the coal industry has been wiped out. Four fairly large collieries were operating and they have folded up. What happens to the people in those communities when an industry is lost? Nothing is put in to replace it, so those people pack up and get out. They are displaced persons. They are not even considered by the immigration department. Perhaps they have an investment of $10,000 or $15,000 in the community, own their own home and so on. They sell out at fire sale prices and wander up into Ontario or into the United States looking for employment. No effort has ever been made by the provincial or federal governments to take a further look at that problem.
I have a telegram here from the secretary of one of our industrial development boards, in the town of Glace Bay. It indicates that another large mine will be closing by the end of May. There are 720 people employed by that mine, the backbone of the whole community. There is a lot of investment based on that mine. It is closing, and there is no social responsibility on the part of that company which has taken millions of dollars of wealth out of this community. The company says the mine will close and that is the end of it. This is a huge corporation with all kinds of research facilities. You would imagine that if that kind of catastrophe were about to take place in such a community the corporation would have been doing some thinking about how the industry could be replaced. They say that is not their problem; they have no responsibility to the human being. They are in business to have figures on the right side of the ledger, so that community is being allowed to fold up.
I have said this a good many times. First the provincial government has to be persuaded that the right to preside over the liquidation of the coal industry should be relinquished. That is all they are doing, presiding over its liquidation. I have been connected with the coal industry for a long time. The only time it ever functioned

properly was during the last war, when the federal government took over the regulation and marketing of coal. It functioned very well and there was no trouble. A lot of standards were raised, pension plans were established, vacations with pay and so forth. When the war was over these things were lost and conditions returned to what they are today.
There is only one answer, Mr. Speaker, to the future of the coal industry. I do not want to be too long about this, but if you read the material that is available concerning what coal may mean to the future of this country, you will be amazed. Remember that natural gas and oil resources are expendable. We have no guarantee how long they are going to last. People who are looking a long way ahead claim that in the final analysis we will have to go back to the coal industry, even as a source for gasoline and a lot of other ingredients that are in that fuel.
For a long time the argument has been that this should be a national industry. Someone will say that under the British North America Act the resources belong to the provinces. That is quite true. At the same time, under the British North America Act the federal government has the power to declare any work in Canada a work of national importance, and they can take over that industry and make it a national industry. Even the little mine at Flin Flon, Manitoba, because it was half in Saskatchewan and half in Manitoba, was taken over by the federal government. The federal government even assumed jurisdiction over labour relations.
People like the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), as well as other people on the front benches, if they have taken any kind of look at all at the operation of the coal industry in Nova Scotia, must have concluded that it has been a faulty operation over the years. I do not think myself that the corporation-actually it consists of about 36 other subsidiaries, many of which are bigger than the coal industry-ever seriously considered trying to market the coal. Marketing is the big problem. The only agency in Canada that can arrange for the marketing of that coal outside of Canada is the federal government. It is beyond the jurisdiction of the provincial government.
A few days ago I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys why the consumer subsidy of $2.40 per ton on coal going into Newfoundland had been discontinued. If applied to 250,000 tons of coal it would mean about half a million dollars. At that time the minister kind of shrugged it off.
The Budget-Mr. Gillis Since then 1 have seen statements in the newspapers by coal dealers in Newfoundland which indicated that the company was not trying to hold that market at all. Here is a clipping dated April 5 which indicates that Herbert K. Wyatt, managing director of the Wyatt Coal and Salt Company, gives the company a terrific beating. He says they had no marketing facilities and no storage facilities for the coal when it went into the car 90 miles away. Their loading facilities were such that they had to drop the coal 80 feet down into the car so that it was pulverized. It is stated that because of the lack of facilities for getting the coal into Newfoundland and marketing it, $3 per ton was added to the cost. Since the consumer subsidy is not being paid, you are not going to market that coal.
The point I want to make is this. This mine that is being closed now employs about 720 people and produces about 700,000 tons of coal. About 250,000 tons of coal should have been kept going across the gulf into Newfoundland. The general manager gave as his reason for closing the mine that they had lost a market for half a million tons of coal and they had not been able to make it up in the past year. At the same time he has a market for 250,000 tons of coal at his back door which he has thrown away because he will not market the coal properly in competition with United States coal.
These are matters that are the responsibility of the government. They are the responsibility of the provincial government first, and second, of the federal government. Every year the federal government puts a substantial amount of money into that industry by way of subvention. Under the Atlantic coal operators' loan arrangement, which went through this house, $10 million was made available and Dosco got $7 [DOT] 5 million to put into a mechanization program. I said ten years ago that so far as mechanization was concerned, and putting heavy electrical equipment in these mines, it was a lot of nonsense and amounted to throwing money down the drain. This contention has proven correct. It has added to the difficulties, in my judgment, and has been largely responsible for the closing of some of these mines. Nevertheless they went ahead with it, and the federal government has that investment.
A lot of the money you lent Dosco under that bill went into its 1-B colliery. It is the one they tried to test that equipment in, and the one they are closing at the present time. So I say the federal government has an investment in it, and I say that investment was not properly looked after, because under the terms of the bill under which they

The Budget-Mr. Gillis received $7,500,000 three specific things were mentioned. First of all it had to be sound from an engineering standpoint and, in my judgment, it was not. Secondly, it had to be economically sound. Well, facts have proven that it was not. And, third, it had to be in the best interests of the community. The mine is being scrapped, and the interests of the community are shot.
The provisions of that bill were never enforced, so far as the federal government is concerned. The dominion coal board have competent engineers who should have watched that project. The federal government should have intervened before these mines were wrecked. That is another responsibility of the federal government.
This Dominion Coal Company, which is supposed to be producing Canadian coal for sale in Canada or anywhere else, is one of the largest importers of United States coal in this country. They have a wholly-owned subsidiary in the city of Montreal known as the Dominion Coal Import Company. This same company which is alleged to be operating coal mines in Nova Scotia, taking out coal to be marketed in Canada, has that big import company which is importing United States coal and filling the markets in the Montreal and Ontario areas that should have been filled with their own coal.

speechtext: The digging of coal does not make you an expert on the marketing of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know a lot about marketing it, too. I have had to go into that angle of it. I am trying to show you that the people who have it, and who take government money, are not looking after it. This is free enterprise.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You don't talk sense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is all balled up under your system.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The only time it functions is during a war, the same as the rest of your economy. It always amuses me to hear members of the Conservative party, particularly, get up in the house and talk about unemployment. Why, today you are just getting back to normal. What we have now is normal during peacetime. There is not a thing wrong that a little war would not cure, not a thing. That is all that is needed. But you never have been able to make this system work, at least during my lifetime, except when there has been a war.
Take a look at the years between 1918 and 1939, and from 1945 to date. It is the same old system: no profits, no work. The solution you offer to get rid of your piled-up inventory is to put the poor men on the street and then come in and say to the government, "You can feed them", after they have broken their backs producing food for somebody else.
I say the federal government granted permission to the Dominion Steel and Coal company to set up a subsidiary in Montreal to import United States coal, and that that permission should be withdrawn. They should be forced to market their own coal in their own market. That is the responsibility of the federal government.
Recently when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Nova Scotia he said there was little hope held for a national coal policy. Well, I think that is pretty shortsighted. Today we have oil, natural gas, atomic energy and coal, all competing with one another. And you mark what I am telling you; just leave them alone for another ten years and you will have neither gas nor oil nor coal, because they will kill one another.

Just take a look at the pipe-line situation- just a stock market promotion, with somebody else paying for it. They are not interested in supplying coal, gas and oil to this country in the future. It is just something to make money out of at the present time.
If we are going to plan the future fuel requirements of this country, then in the light of the situation today a national body should be set up, composed of competent people who know marketing conditions and who are familiar with these fuels, so that the future of Canada in the matter of fuel supplies may be protected.
Just take a look at what happened during the last war down in the Windsor area, where they were receiving natural gas from the United States. When the Yanks needed it they just shut it off, and you had that whole area running around looking for coal-burning equipment and trying to get coal supplies. That can happen again. The main lines from which we are pumping oil today are in the United States; they are not in this country. It often amuses me to hear people talk about the United States, and the possibility of war with us. They do not have to have a war with us; all they have to do is shut off the fuel supply and we are finished. Industries and everything else would stop.
It is time we began to take a square look at this question. I know they are doing what they can in the maritime provinces, but geography is against them. A development is taking place there today that will pay dividends. The formation of the Atlantic economic council is something that should have been done 25 years ago, because the answer to the maritimes' problem is in the interprovincial marketing development and complementing the economy of each part of that section of the country. Following that is the development of industry in the communities, where they are taking advantage of the research being done at the provincial level. They are setting up funds, not to bring money in but to create it in the communities and to control it there. If that development continues, then in my judgment in five or six years you will not be sending very much to the maritime provinces from Ontario and Quebec. They will be supplying you.
That is the kind of job that has to be done. But at the present time, and until such time as they can get something done for themselves, the federal and provincial governments at the next dominion-provincial conference should take a look at the coal
The Budget-Mr. Gillis industry, because much of it can still be salvaged. In my judgment, however, it has to be taken out of the hands of people who merely use it as a means of pressuring the federal government into sending them out more money. That is the way it has been working in that industry as long as I can remember.
Let me conclude by saying this, that so far as the budget is concerned, it is as good as I expected it would be.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps you did not expect much.

speechtext:
It is as good as I expected. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) offered the criticisms on behalf of this group, and I do not wish to take time to repeat them. He did it better than I could. But I think the time is coming in this country when there should be two budgets. First of all the Minister of Finance should do the sort of thing he did on April 5. He should give us a bookkeeping review of the year's activities, and a statement as to what he thinks his deficit or surplus will be in the next year. He could also give a forecast of what he would expect in the following year.
In addition to that there should be a capital budget. What is wrong in this country today is that we have no objectives. We have nothing to work for. If the Minister of Finance could bring in a capital budget and say, "Our objective next year is to clean up the slums of Canada so far as it is possible in each and every city, and also we are going to establish a system of low-rental subsidized housing to that end," in a very few months time you would have unemployment licked, and you would have every honest member in the house out working for you to complete that program and attain that objective.
This is not the way to build a country. I hope the next time the minister brings in his budget he will also have a capital budget. He is pretty realistic and I would hope he might do this, so that he would be able to tell the house, as his white paper said in 1945, "These are our objectives for the building of industry, the development of our resources and the housing of our people. If we cannot find risk capital to do this during this year, we shall do it ourselves by using the facilities that we have in the Bank of Canada." I hope we shall be able to do that at the next session.
On motion of Mr. Hahn the debate was adjourned.
